item.title: Checklist
item.description:
Production checklist#

This checklist is for you if you install or operate the materialize-monitoring stack in production. It covers the collection tier (Alloy), node metrics (node-exporter), and the bundled Loki, Thanos, Grafana, and Alertmanager.

The checklist is ordered by what goes wrong if you skip an item, most severe first:

Exposure
Someone outside the trust boundary can read your data or change your configuration.
Silent failure
Part of the stack stops working without an error, so nothing tells you.
Data loss
An ordinary restart, node loss, or upgrade loses telemetry or state for good.
Outage
Part of the stack fails to install, upgrade, or stay up. These failures are loud.
Capacity and cost
The stack runs short of resources, or costs more than it needs to.
Hardening and extras
Nothing breaks. Each item adds defense in depth, or extra signal where your environment calls for it.

Each item is tagged with its owner under the shared responsibility model, and names the component it touches. The component links to the page that explains the setting. Open items are yours to act on. What the chart already ships is checked, and collapsed at the end of each tier.

item.title: Stack-wide settings
item.description:
Stack-wide settings#

This page explains the settings that cut across every component: the namespace layout, scheduling priority, network policies, image registries, and the zone count. What to do about each one is in the production checklist, ordered by what goes wrong if you skip it.

Namespace layout#

Each subchart uses a deterministic name, a static fullnameOverride such as loki or thanos, so no resource carries a release-name prefix. That assumes one instance of each backend per namespace, which is a reasonable constraint for an umbrella infrastructure chart. Two layouts are supported; both are fine, so pick per your isolation needs.

item.title: Collection (Alloy)
item.description:
Collection (Alloy)#

The Alloy tier collects and processes telemetry before it reaches a backend. It runs in two roles: the alloy-agent DaemonSet, one per node, and the alloy-gateway Deployment. Both are configured as code; for more information, see the logging pipeline reference. The gateway holds the dominant cost and stability lever, so most of the care goes there.

This page explains how the tier behaves. What to do about it is in the production checklist.

item.title: Node metrics (node-exporter)
item.description:
Node metrics (node-exporter)#

node-exporter is a DaemonSet that reads the host kernel and exposes what no other collector in this stack sees: swap, memory pressure, node-level network counters, disk I/O, conntrack, and clock sync. The Alloy gateway scrapes it through the ServiceMonitor the subchart ships. For where it sits in the stack, see Architecture. What to do about it is in the production checklist.

It’s a separate workload on purpose, and not folded into the Alloy agent even though Alloy’s prometheus.exporter.unix is the same program. Keeping them apart keeps their resource limits apart. Sharing one envelope means a metrics regression starves log collection, which is the signal you most need during the incident it caused. Separate DaemonSets also have independent eviction and can be excluded from specific node pools. The trade accepted in exchange is one more per-node workload.

item.title: Metrics (Thanos)
item.description:
Metrics (Thanos)#

This page explains how the bundled Thanos is replicated, sized, spread, and stored, and why. For the architecture these settings configure, see Metrics architecture. What to do about them is in the production checklist.

Receive replication#

Replication, not receive.mode, is the availability lever. It’s the single most consequential setting, and the one most often misread.

receive.mode is a topology choice:

  • standalone (default) is RouterIngestor mode — one workload that both routes and ingests. It still builds a ketama hashring across the StatefulSet pods (receive.hashrings.autogen), so replicaCount: 3 shards writes across three pods.
  • split separates Router (Deployment) from Ingester (StatefulSet) so they scale independently.

Neither choice, by itself, gives you redundancy. The replication factor does. The subchart passes --receive.replication-factor only in split mode, so standalone would run at Thanos’s default of 1. This chart sets it to 3 through receive.extraArgs instead, which is the shape the following example shows.

item.title: Grafana
item.description:
Grafana#

This page explains what separates the bundled Grafana’s defaults from a production Grafana. For the architecture these settings configure, see Grafana architecture. What to do about them is in the production checklist.

Grafana is the one component here that isn’t a data store, and that changes what “production” means for it. Nothing observable is lost when Grafana breaks. The metrics are in Thanos, the logs are in Loki, and grafana-operator re-pushes the dashboards this chart installs every resyncPeriod. What is at risk is everything a human created through the UI, plus the fact that Grafana is where an incident starts.

item.title: Alertmanager
item.description:
Alertmanager#

This page explains how the bundled Alertmanager is shaped for production. For the architecture these settings configure, see Alert architecture, and for routing and receivers, see Alert channels. What to do about them is in the production checklist.

Alertmanager is the one component in this stack whose failure is silent by construction. A notifier that’s down, partitioned, or misconfigured produces no alert about itself, and the absence of a page reads the same as the absence of a problem. So the defaults target surviving a bad day rather than a minimal footprint, and the validators concentrate on the configurations that fail quietly.
